Glossary

    Examples · IGL

    Words: 1355

    Six decisions for the “I decide whether a script should exist at all” level. Here code illustrates the decision rather than the reverse: the task of this level is forecasting the total cost of ownership one year out.

    Key idea of this page #

    At this level, the primary question is not “how to write it,” but “should we write it, and what will it cost us down the road.” The most expensive script in any team's history is the one that successfully solved the wrong problem: taking on state management, acquiring a custom state file, and accumulating custom state reconciliation bugs. The six analyses below focus on architectural choices rather than syntax: when to refuse to write a script; what interface contract to establish when a script becomes a machine-callable tool; how to survive retries in distributed environments; what telemetry a script must emit; how to bound worst-case blast radius; and how to safely decommission a script when its lifecycle ends. That final decommissioning step is skipped most often - yet it is what separates engineering discipline from ad-hoc scripting. Each case study includes a “Decision cost” analysis: the cost of implementing versus the cost of avoiding.

    1 · The decision not to write a script #

    Situation: The team requests a “quick script” to monitor state and reconcile drift.

    # what is requested:
# - inspect what is deployed
# - diff against desired state
# - converge to desired state
# - record actions taken

# this describes Terraform,
# not a shell script
    Why so: State convergence, declarative idempotence, and resource diffing live beyond the proper boundaries of Bash. If you attempt to solve them in shell scripts, you will inevitably invent your own state files, custom object diffing, and buggy partial failure handling. The mature engineering decision is to step back from shell scripting and adopt purpose-built tools like Ansible or Terraform where this orchestration is fully solved. Remember: the most expensive script you can write is one that successfully solves the wrong problem.
    Decision cost: Declining costs a single conversation and perhaps a week evaluating a dedicated tool. Agreeing commits to indefinite maintenance of an in-house state management engine - with costs scaling directly with managed resource count.

    2 · Tool contract: scripts for machines #

    Situation: Your script will be invoked by downstream scripts, CI pipelines, and automated agents - machines rather than humans.

    # contract to declare explicitly:
# stdout   - results only
# stderr   - all diagnostics and logs
# 0        - success
# 1        - expected domain failure
# 2        - invalid command invocation
# 3-63     - custom codes, documented in --help
# 126, 127, 128+N - reserved by shell
# --json   - machine-readable output
# --dry-run - non-destructive execution
    Why so: When you build command-line tools for other software to consume, contract stability matters far more than implementation details: you can always refactor internal code, but external programs depend strictly on your interface. Differentiate between routine negative outcomes ("resource not found") and fatal crashes: callers should handle the former gracefully while the latter must stop pipelines. Support an explicit --json flag so you can refine human-readable terminal output without breaking automated machine parsers. When selecting exit codes, align with sysexits.h (64 for invalid usage, 70 for internal software failure, 75 for temporary outages). Never occupy codes 126, 127, or 128+N: the shell reserves these, and callers will be unable to distinguish your tool failure from "command not executable", "command not found", or fatal OS signal crashes.
    Decision cost: Formalizing the contract costs thirty minutes and a dozen lines in --help. Omitting it turns every future output edit into an outage for callers you may not even know exist.

    3 · Idempotence and retry resilience in distributed environments #

    Situation: A job is triggered by a scheduler that upon hitting a timeout fires a retry without waiting for the prior run to complete.

    # not idempotent:
echo "$line" >> report.txt
counter=$((counter + 1))

# idempotent:
key="run-$(date +%F)-$id"
grep -q "^$key" done.log || {
  work "$id"
  echo "$key" >> done.log
}
    Why so: In distributed architectures, re-running your automation is a normal operational reality: network timeouts, container evictions, and duplicate queue deliveries happen constantly. Design idempotence so repeated executions converge on desired state without side effects. Assign a unique operation identifier and execute state mutations only when that key has not been processed. Pay close attention to concurrency limits: testing with grep followed by echo is not atomic; if your system experiences parallel access, introduce file locking or an external datastore - a clear signal that your problem has outgrown shell scripting.
    Decision cost: An idempotency key and completion log require ten lines. Without them, scheduler retries produce duplicate billings, duplicate notification blasts, or destructive repeated deletions.

    4 · Observability: what scripts must emit #

    Situation: A script runs unattended overnight, and its outcome is only reviewed twenty-four hours later.

    start=$(date +%s)
trap 'report "$?" "$start"' EXIT

report() {
  local rc=$1 t=$(( $(date +%s) - $2 ))
  printf 'result=%s rc=%s sec=%s items=%s\n' \
    "$([ "$rc" = 0 ] && echo ok || echo fail)" \
    "$rc" "$t" "$count" >&2
}
    Why so: Without telemetry, you will only detect that your script has degraded when it catastrophically crashes in production. Emit at least four core metrics - outcome status, exit code, execution duration, and items processed: with these, you can graph trends and catch resource starvation before it becomes an outage. Simple key-value log formats are easily ingested by metrics collectors without complex regexes. And emitting metrics via an EXIT trap guarantees your observability pipeline receives telemetry even when your script terminates abnormally.
    Decision cost: One structured line emitted per execution. Without it, performance degradation remains hidden until complete failure occurs - usually discovered by customers first.

    5 · Blast radius: bounding worst-case failure modes #

    Situation: A script purges aged resources. The question is not “does it work,” but “what happens when its logic fails.”

    # restrict execution outside allowed scope
case "$target" in
  /opt/app/releases/*) ;;
  *) echo "out of scope: $target" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# cap work per single invocation
if (( ${#list[@]} > 20 )); then
  echo "too many items" >&2
  exit 2
fi
    Why so: Constrain blast radius in your automation with two defensive boundaries. A strict path whitelist prevents accidental deletions outside targeted directories, even if your environment variable expands empty or a search filter misbehaves. A hard batch limit on modified resources per run turns catastrophic outages into contained incidents: a script that resolves a thousand resources for deletion instead of five should halt immediately and alert you. Design your shell scripts against the absolute worst-case failure rather than the happy path.
    Decision cost: Two validation checks at script initialization. Without them, a single filtering typo risks destroying everything within the script's ambient IAM permissions.

    6 · Decommissioning scripts gracefully #

    Situation: Legacy script functionality has migrated into a platform tool, but dependent callers continue invoking the original entry point.

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "DEPRECATED: use 'app deploy'" >&2
echo "this script will be decommissioned 2026-12-01" >&2

exec app deploy "$@"   # proxying for now
    Why so: You can never deprecate a production script overnight: team pipelines, cross-department cron jobs, and ingrained engineer habits depend on it. Implement a proxying deprecation phase with an explicit sunset date: this affords your consumers runway to migrate and leaves audit trails in logs so you can trace remaining traffic. Always specify a deadline in deprecation warnings: open-ended obsolescence notices are ignored for years. Thorough retirement workflows distinguish mature engineering from quick hacks.
    Decision cost: A month of proxying and reviewing invocation logs. Skipping this step guarantees breaking uncataloged dependencies on the day of removal.

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Six architectural decisions evaluated before code is written. Your time was well spent if before approving your next script you ask “what happens when its filter fails” and “who will decommission this when it is superseded.” That is the essence of rewiring: accountability shifts from immediate functionality to long-term blast radius, defining the boundary between an implementer and a technical lead.

    1. Signs of misplaced scope: inspect, diff, converge, record - this belongs in state engines.
    2. Tool contracts: dedicated streams, exit code semantics, --json, --dry-run - avoiding shell reserved codes 126, 127, and 128+N.
    3. Idempotency keys to survive distributed scheduler retries.
    4. Four core telemetry metrics: outcome status, exit code, duration, processed count.
    5. Scope whitelists and batch caps: bounding failure blast radius.
    6. Dated proxying phases when deprecating and retiring scripts.
